More recently, we’ve learned that evolution did not optimize chickens for growing the largest breasts in the shortest possible time, or for laying the most eggs; agricultural genetics companies have made massive strides in these areas in a short time.

Now, reader, what about happiness? General wellbeing? How useful were positive vs. negative affective states in the evolutionary environment?

We all know what physical pain was useful for: motivating our ancestors to avoid bodily harms that could erase their chances of reproducing. The same goes for hunger, thirst, etc. Enjoyable physical feelings are just the opposite, a reward for doing things that increase your reproductive potential.

With enough time—which there definitely was—we should expect these evolutionary signals to converge on a mathematical optimum. Things should hurt in proportion to the amount they reduce your chance of reproduction, and feel good in proportion to the amount they increase it. No meal can increase your reproductive odds as much as, well, reproducing, so no meal is as pleasurable as consensual sex– unless you’re on the brink of starvation, in which case eating could unlock a whole lifetime of reproductive opportunities; that meal should beat the best sex of your life.

Now I ask you: on net, would this evolutionary mathematics favor pain, or suffering? What should we expect to find if we add them all up over the course of each life, or across the sum of all lives?

The obvious answer might seem like at least zero; things should balance out. I think this is wrong.

Try to see things from evolution’s point of view. (OK, evolution is a blind idiot god, it doesn’t see anything; still, try to empathize with whatever senses it does possess.) From that vantage point, what good are contented organisms? They don’t do anything to improve their odds of reproducing; they just sit there. Worthless!

No, contentment is only useful as a lure. Evolution wants to give its organisms just enough contentment to know it is possible, then pull it away, dangle it out in front of them so they will chase after it, leading them in the directions it wants them to go.

There are countless things in nature that can wipe away your reproductive fitness in a short time. A pack of hyenas tear you limb from limb; screwworms infest an open wound, devouring you from the inside; a bacterial infection spreads through your blood, slowly annihilating you; you slip and fall down a ravine, breaking your legs and starving to death.

Almost nothing can double your fitness in the same amount of time. One sexual act doesn’t come close. Being rescued from the ravine, fed, and having your legs put back together might come close, if it had ever happened in our ancestral environment.

There is a common belief that widespread anxiety and depression today must be some kind of maladaptation to modern life, a mismatch between our evolutionary conditioning and our new social environment, our removal from small tight-knit communities into a vast impersonal society. Nature, the thinking goes, would never design beings that are just miserable by default.

No, man, that’s exactly what nature did! Anxiety isn’t a mistake, it’s nature’s first resort for motivating you. Anxiety is the feeling that you might lose something if you don’t act; depression is a blunt tool for teaching you to act differently next time if you did lose something. As psychiatrist Randy Nesse explained in an interview on 80,000 Hours:

[You might think] natural selection would shape us for health and happiness and cooperation and long, happy lives... once you start studying how evolution shapes behaviour-regulation mechanisms, you realise that it doesn’t give a damn.

Imagine you’re getting water for your family at the watering hole on the savanna, and it’s evening and you hear a noise behind a rock… Pretend that the cost of running is 100 calories, and you always get away free. And pretend that if you don’t run, you are eaten by a lion, and that’s about 100,000 calories. The ratio is about 1,000 to one. Whoa. So that means that anytime the noise is loud enough to indicate the probability a lion is there is greater than one in 1,000, you should run. And that means that 999 times, a normal reaction will be a false alarm… These systems are shaped to give off many, many false alarms.

From a standpoint of evolutionary incentives, it’s a miracle that any of us is anything other than a ball of fear and anxiety!

Generating mercy

All of this is good news for helping farmed animals. Pain, anxiety, and depression—the fundamental machinery of misery for animals in factory farms—aren’t just accidents of evolution, they are its key instruments, tools it has optimized over the course of millions of years. I said it would be easy to improve on things evolution wasn’t trying to improve on, but what about going in the exact opposite direction? That should be even easier. Destruction is easier than creation; all we have to do is smash nature’s precious little torture devices into a thousand pieces.

To this day, animal genetics companies are selectively breeding farmed animals to try to increase their profitability: how fast they grow, their resistance to common pathogens, and their ability to survive the unnatural conditions inside factory farms. What if along with those efforts, we selected animals who suffer less? Who feel less pain, fear, and anxiety, or even none at all? Who feel instead contentment, bliss, and physical comfort in what for others would be the worst conditions? How many generations do you think it would take to breed animals who genuinely love life inside factory farms?

While you estimate, note that in humans or wild animals, tending too far in this direction would be disastrous. Some amount of pain is necessary feedback from your body. Nesse again:

We saw a patient who had no capacity for pain. And he was a wreck. He was a smoker and his fingers were burned right down to the bone, because he didn’t know... It’s extremely rare — one out of several hundred thousand people. And why is it rare? Because most people with that syndrome are dead by the time they’re age 30 or 40. Pain itself is useful.

Anxiety is just the psychosocial analog of pain. Nesse describes patients who lacked any anxiety as similarly impaired. One was a professional motorcycle racer in a sport where 10% of participants die every year. Another always said what was on her mind, exhibiting the lack of social anxiety many of us dream of, and alienating all her friends in the process.

On the other hand, there’s the story of Jo Cameron. By her account, Jo has likely never felt pain, describing everything from giving birth to breaking bones in a car wreck as “a tickle.” She is also apparently immune to anxiety and depression, yet has lived a cheerful and functional life into her seventies. In 2019, researchers attributed her anaesthesia to specific genetic mutations, some of which she passed onto her son, who experiences reduced pain but not to the same degree as Jo. Her case is rare but not fully unique; the Marsilis family likewise leads happy lives with broken bones causing at most a few seconds of discomfort.

If pain-free humans can live happy lives out in the wild, animals in highly controlled factory farm settings have much less to lose. We could even imagine animals who prefer the safety and immobility of a battery cage to the uncertainty of an open cage-free barn where they are more likely to be injured. But then, without pain or anxiety, maybe they won’t care one way or another if they get injured.

So, how many generations do you think it would take to wreck evolution’s careful handiwork of pain and anxiety in selectively bred chickens? Well, nobody has tried, but looking at similar breeding efforts can give us a clue. Starting in the 1950s, a Russian team starting from wild foxes bred a fully docile domestic house fox—tail wagging, potty trainable—in ten generations. An ag geneticist in the 90s cut the rate of mortality in battery cage hens from 68% to 9% by eliminating cannibalism in just six generations.

Experts in the movement are starting to estimate that if they set their hearts to it, genetics companies could eliminate the most extreme negative affects in a handful of breeding generations—just a few years for most species—and basically eliminate suffering within at most a few dozen.

What’s stopping us? Returning to our venn diagram, it’s not producers. Factory farms have no actual desire for animals to be tortured. If anything, happier animals could be more cooperative. If this were folded into existing breeding optimization programs, the cost would be low and the effects would cascade by default into nearly every factory farm in the world.

Neither, for now, is regulation a problem. Public opinion might be. But the most immediate obstacle is advocates. We haven’t embraced this path yet, because we haven’t yet given up on more aesthetically satisfying approaches.

Well, if you’re squirming now, we’d better cut to the chase.

Rung 3: Genetically engineered happy chickens

The hardest thing about increasing animal welfare through selective breeding—besides the moral reckoning it poses to advocates and the public— will probably be measurement. To decide which individuals to breed in each generation, we need to know which ones are happier. It would be easy if they could just tell us, like Jo Cameron. Until and unless we solve that problem (lots of people seem excited about human-animal communication with AI) then we’ll need to rely on some other measurement.

This will quickly bring us face to face with Goodhart’s law: when a proxy measurement becomes an optimization target, it ceases to be useful as a measurement.

Ask yourself: how could we tell which chicken is happier or more miserable than her sisters inside a factory farm? We might measure the concentration of cortisol and other stress hormones in their blood, the frequency and tone of their vocalizations, or the strength of their preference for water laced with analgesics. In a single generation, all of these might be good indicators. But as soon as we start selecting for them, we have no easy way of knowing whether we’re actually breeding happier animals, or just animals who talk more and are unaffected by ibuprofen.

Subjective experience is unlike other factors animal geneticists have optimized for until now. There’s no risk of Goodhart smiting you if all you care about is giant breasts. Goodhart only awakens when the measurement you’re using is a proxy for the thing you care about rather than the thing itself.

I’m quite confident that with careful effort, we could solve this problem and select for happier farmed animals. But there might be a simpler solution. Selective breeding is, famously, not the only way to modify genes.

Consider Jo Cameron’s genome. (Thankfully, scientists have.) We have the technology now to isolate the mutations responsible for her painless state with a high degree of confidence, and a few generations of experimentation would be enough to confirm it with near certainty. We also already have the technology to insert those genes into another person, who will then pass them on to all their own offspring.

What good are these human genes for chickens? A lot, it turns out. Pain is very old; humans share most of our pain genes with most animals, and even more with most vertebrates. (Heck, we share 60% of our genes with bananas; nature doesn’t fix what ain’t broken.) If our pain genes date back long enough, then Jo’s mutations would have a similar effect on nearly all farmed species.

Preliminary experiments support this hope: inserting the mutant genes of the painless Marsili family caused mice to show behavioral signs consistent with pain reduction. Studies have achieved similar results by genetically knocking out nociceptor development in chickens and even flies. And unlike with selective breeding, these measures seem reliable since the intervention wasn’t targeting the observable behaviors but the pain itself, as reported by the humans the genes were borrowed from.

Across most of the animal kingdom, we know of a few dozen genetic markers that play a large role in pain and other negative affective states. This gives us a fairly high-resolution dial; we could turn pain down as much as we want. Fully eliminating it is on the table, but so is leaving just enough to stop animals maiming themselves without realizing.

Should we do it?

If you feel unsure about whether animals could be genetically engineered for happiness and low suffering, picture a golden retriever.

Now, suppose I told you that the farming of dogs for meat in China was not going anywhere anytime soon; in fact, it’s only going to grow in the years to come, and there’s nothing you or anyone else can do about it. But you do have one choice: you could convince every dog farmer in China to replace their current breeds with golden retrievers.

At first, this seems like an abomination: to take beings with so much potential for joy and pack them into the worst imaginable hell feels even more atrocious than doing it to less happy animals.

But slow down, use your thinking brain. The question is not whether a golden retriever will live free or in a farm. The question is whether the dog in a farm will be a golden retriever or a less happy breed. There is not a finite number of golden retrievers; filling China’s farms with them won’t reduce the number of happy ones.

The fact that golden retrievers are so much happier than other dogs in domestic life doesn’t necessarily mean that they’d be happier than other dogs inside of factory farms. But the plan proposed here doesn’t have that problem; we would be designing animals specifically to thrive inside factory farms. Beings utterly devoid of negative affect, for whom every moment lying still in the ammonia-choked air is pure bliss, for whom even the blade cutting into their throat feels like an orgasm. In the limit, maybe these animals would be happier in factory farms than they could be anywhere else.

One severe welfare problem in aquaculture farms is water quality. Fishes and shrimps are packed in so densely that the oxygen levels drop low enough to be toxic, and the sludge of excrement and rotting excess food never gets cleared away. What do you think would happen if an environment like this arose in nature? Well, over a long enough time, some organisms would evolve to thrive on it; they’d adapt to need less oxygen and perhaps even thrive on this water. This exact principle could be used to selectively breed shrimps and fishes who don’t mind the poor water quality. In fact, experiments like this have already happened: give shrimps access to a pool where the oxygen is much higher in some areas than others. Most of the shrimps cluster in the high oxygen areas, but some hang out in the hypoxic areas. Select only those shrimps and soon all their descendants seem indifferent about where in the pool to hang out.

Is this experimental setup vulnerable to Goodharting? As described, absolutely. Maybe all the shrimps prefer oxygen, but some prefer solitude even more. This would perfectly backfire, selecting shrimps who don’t like company for life in densely packed farms. This uncertainty is why going straight to editing on the genetic level is so appealing.

Well, appealing to… whom exactly?

The public will be put in a strange position by the prospect of genetically engineered happy animals. Some people have managed to convince themselves that the animals they eat are already happy; others are genuinely distressed by the violence of meat and must actively try not to think about it when shopping. If we could offer people a future where they could truly eat cheap meat without guilt, would it be enough to overcome the naturalism bias?

Maybe not right away. Public discomfort with genetic engineering was enough to derail golden rice, a cultivar rich in vitamin A that could be preventing 10,000s of children a year from dying in low-income countries and 100,000s more from going blind but has instead been tied up in frivolous lawsuits by Greenpeace.

Public opposition to genetic engineering in food is the strongest reason to think selective breeding might go further than genetic engineering, at least in the short term. You can imagine the headline: Tech bros want to genetically engineer your dinner. Never mind the genetic war crimes already perpetuated against dinner by the biggest meat companies on earth; they didn’t use CRISPR. (If you’re a journalist reading this 17,000-word post to clip viral sentences from, here’s one for you: you really suck, OK?)

Notably, though, this same resistance might not apply to animals not consumed by humans. Hundreds of millions of rats and mice are factory farmed every year for snake food, and insect farming could still take off. Both could be ideal places to prove genetic engineering. And there is a pathway to market if the stakeholders align; the U.S. FDA has already approved genetically engineered strains of salmon and pigs, and Japanese regulators have greenlit a number of CRISPR-edited fish species.

Notice something about that last sentence: you probably haven’t heard anything about it before. The USDA approving, in April 2025, an intervention genetically engineering pigs for resistance to Porcine Reproductive and Respiratory Syndrome was the most significant regulatory decision on genetic engineering in a decade. It generated a quiet buzz in industry trade press, and nowhere else. If it had gone viral and been subsumed into the culture war, it easily could have fallen prey to the cottage industry of MAHA luddite influencers constantly on the prowl to make their follower count go brrr by exposing the latest global elite conspiracy.

The ag industry has no obvious reason to oppose either selective breeding or genetic engineering for welfare as long as neither interferes with productivity or demand. In fact, happy animals could be more docile and cooperative. But an even bigger carrot might be never having to deal with animal activists ever again. And that would be the arrangement: if you get behind this, and let us verify it’s actually working rather than Goodharting, then we will never again run ads against you, show up outside your houses at 2 am with bullhorns, or sneak into your farms to take footage and rescue animals. We’d have no need to. We’ll be the ones most vocally advocating for these innovations when regulators and consumers have questions.

That just leaves animal advocates. Can we bring ourselves to make a deal with the devil? Should we?

It’s OK to feel squeamish about all this. A version of me from even just a year or two ago would have been horrified by all this. I wish I could put my finger on exactly what changed for me; if I could, maybe it wouldn’t have taken so many words to get this far.

Maybe you feel that genetically subjugating animals to our will is an even worse violation on top of subjugating them physically. That it could lock in a morally bleak situation for much longer instead of trying to outright end it.

Or, maybe you think suffering is redemptive, a key part of a meaningful life. You wouldn’t want someone to take away your capacity for complex experiences, to turn you into a passive blob of happy flesh waiting contentedly to be slaughtered.

Maybe your suffering is meaningful, and I wouldn’t try to take it away from you. But this just clearly is not true for animals in factory farms. Even if they had the cognitive ability to do so—and it’s not at all clear that they do—they have no opportunity to transmute their pain into meaning. The right thing for you is not necessarily the right thing for an animal who will only ever exist trapped inside a factory farm, waiting to die.

But if, in the end, you just can’t let go of the sense that this is a violation of some inalienable right to genetic sovereignty, that such a violation is worse than all the torture—and I’m not trying to be snide here, there are coherent moral worldviews in which this is true—if that’s where you land, then I have one last solution I know you’ll love.

Rung 4: Brainless chickens

Let’s not sugarcoat it: we’re talking about chicken bodies (or pigs, fishes, etc) with beating hearts, lungs, nerves, everything. Just no brain. In the place of a brain is a bundle of cables connecting the body to a computer. The computer sends signals to inflate and deflate the lungs, beat the heart, and exercise the muscles that will eventually be sold as meat. The spinal cord is hijacked just before it would reach the brainstem, which does not exist and never existed. Tubes pump food, water, and necessary hormones down the esophagus. The body lies shoulder to shoulder on a rack of identical brainless bodies stretching far as the eye can see in all six directions– which isn’t very far because there is no light in here other than pathogen-killing UVC, and there are no eyes to see and—most importantly—nobody to do the seeing.

Nobody is home inside this factory farm. It is perfectly peaceful. No happiness, no pain, nobody to have their genetic sovereignty violated.

If you were excited about cultivated meat, you have no reason to oppose this. This might just be what cost-competitive cultivated meat production looks like in the end; bioreactors made not of metal, but of skin and bones. Bodies growing like fruits on a mechanical tree. Meat without suffering, engineered in reverse. The technological genie grants our wishes, just not how we expected.

Imagine for a moment that you’re a bullet-biting utilitarian. You chomp down repugnant conclusions for breakfast. You want to fill the universe with happy experiences– as many and as happy as possible. This requires two steps: first, figuring out how to produce happy lives, and second, marshalling resources to do it. You discover a sequence of genes that produces beings who live joyful, euphoric lives in literally any conditions; they simply cannot help but have an amazing time. Excitedly, you rush to publish your paper.

But when the paper comes out, nobody cares. To your immense frustration and confusion, nobody is willing to start spending all of society’s resources manufacturing breeding facilities for your joyful homonculi. You go back to the library and ask Claude:

Hey Claude, how do people manage to get stuff done in society? Like, what gets society to expend resources on some things and not other things?

You’re pretty bright—you just invented a genetic organism from scratch, after all—so you pick up Claude’s economics lesson quickly. You know exactly what to do. You go back, make a few tweaks, and publish your new paper.

This time, you have a sequence of genes that produce happy animals who poop out cheap chicken breast.

You find an investor. With their investment, you build your first happy animal lab. The animals lead joyous lives, equally happy in an open field or stuffed into a drawer, so the most ethical thing is to stuff them all into drawers and make as many as possible. Then, selling the chicken-breast-poop, you fund your second facility. Soon you have a massive, globe-spanning industrial supply chain for producing happy experiences, all funded by consumer demand, and you’re starting to think about interstellar expansion.

Then you hear about a new upstart competitor. Well, you wouldn’t normally think in terms of competition; in your mind, this whole supply chain is about producing happiness, and you’d love for other people to produce even more. But quickly you realize that’s not what this is at all. This new company is trying to undercut your revenue source, without making happy lives. They took the genetic code you had openly published in the hopes others would copy it, and they modified it so that only the body remains. It still poops out chicken breast, but the brain is gone, replaced by a central computer regulating thousands of bodies at once. They’re just in it to make money!

5. Help Wanted

“If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death, and those that are ready to be slain;” – Proverbs 24:11

Will some process of producing meat without sentience inevitably win out in the end, due to the ruthless optimizations of replication? Should we prefer that over any conceivable form of farming with conscious animals, no matter how happy they are engineered to be? Will consumers ever tolerate columns of fleshy meat-vats plugged into a computer if it looks too much like a scene from the matrix?

Mercifully, I don’t think we need to have answers to these questions right now. We just need to take the next step forward. We in particular need you to do that.

One way to understand where welfare tech and welfare genetics fit into the movement is this grid:

There’s always been sufficient technology for society to stop farming animals if it wanted to. But it doesn’t. So we’ve pushed the industry to adopt low-tech welfare improvements while investing our innovative energy in replacing animals altogether. Until now, we haven’t been investing in technologies that make the next welfare improvements more impactful for animals or easier for the industry to adopt.

That’s finally starting to change.

From the outside, it might seem like the EA wing of the animal advocacy movement goes through fads. That’s because it does. In each cycle, funders get excited about a shiny new object, and put out a call for established organizations and new startup founders to rush into that space by making it clear funding will be available for anyone who does. Vegan leafleting was one such fad, followed by corporate cage-free campaigns, then cultivated meat and alternative proteins in general. Politics is the current fad, and welfare innovation will be the next one.

This can be frustrating for people working on an intervention that never gets popular. But that doesn’t mean it’s actually suboptimal. Some of our fads have worked out, and others haven’t; so it goes.

Animal advocates have limited resources, both money and people, spread thin across researchers, campaigners, and grantmakers. It’s probably the case that we needed to put all of our spare energy into cage-free campaigning to get the ball rolling there, and indeed, while the cage-free fight has been a big success, it’s hardly over despite all the energy invested. I’m glad that increasing our political capacity has been a major influence for the last few years and that it will continue to get attention.

But I’m also glad that there’s about to be a major infusion of money and attention into welfare innovation. And because of that, it’s quickly becoming clear that the pace of this innovation will be limited not by funding, but by talent. That’s where you come in.

Start/join a startup

Perhaps the most impactful thing you could do is start a new startup and become the animal movement’s point person on one or more specific technological innovations.

But Aidan, I hear you say, I’m not a mechanical engineer or anything like that. I got my bachelor’s degree in Medieval Studies, with a minor in Puppetry. How am I supposed to start a tech company?

Be not afraid, dear reader. While technical skills would go a long way, not all founders need to be technical. First, there are many technologies that we’ve already pretty much developed, for which the task is now to get them adopted across the industry; that’s a more versatile strategy role.

Second, most of your role as a founder is to communicate a clear vision for your startup, recruit the right people, and get them the resources they need to succeed. You could recruit technical talent from outside the movement if you can demonstrate to funders that you have what it takes to lead.

Third, there has never been a better time to quickly teach yourself skills– and by teach yourself, I mean have ChatGPT or Claude teach you. Anyone willing to learn to use AI agents now has the power of a mediocre software engineer, and with a surprisingly small amount of elbow grease you can become dangerous. Learning mechanical engineering would be a bit steeper for sure, but you can at least teach yourself enough to get by and even to prototype. As Paul Graham says:

If that still sounds scary, there are people whose job it is to help you.

Spring Innovation Fund is a new “not-for-profit venture philanthropy studio and fund built specifically for Welfare Tech,” basically an incubator where you can get expert coaching and seed funding to launch your startup. They have separate tracks for engineers/builders vs. ideators/entrepreneurs, with competitive salaries for the former and up to $500,000 in seed funding for the latter. Learn more and express interest here.

Ambitious Impact (formerly Charity Entrepreneurship) is a longstanding accelerator for high-impact charities. They’re pros and literally wrote the book. AIM has incubated many animal charities in the past, but next year they’re launching their first cohort entirely dedicated to animal welfare, with a focus on welfare innovation. Like Spring, AIM offers an intensive coaching program, cofounders, and seed funding. Learn more and apply here by September 13.

If you want to join an existing organization working in this space, email me and I can share some other high impact opportunities.

Donate

If you’re looking to make a large donation into this space, get in touch and I can point you in the right direction.

Accelerate adoption

What if you’re part of an existing animal advocacy org that isn’t well suited to research? There’s a role for you too, but it will require a greater degree of self-examination.

6. Hope doesn’t replicate

“Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” – Amos 3:3

The most powerful recurring theme in welfare innovation is that there are numerous interventions where the desires of advocates and the industry align, and it is the public or regulators who need to be educated and brought onboard. This is where campaigners can thrive. We can partner with the industry to educate doubters about the need for easy welfare wins like vaccines and high-welfare breeds.

To realize the full potential of technology and genetics for welfare, we’ll need to shift the way we think about friend and foe.

Way back in section 2, I admitted that we can’t know for sure how much impact the meme of animal rights has had on the world. Maybe without it, factory farming would have grown even faster and been even more cruel.

But could it have been net negative? Lately I’ve been wondering what the world might look like if animal advocates and factory farmers had never wound up in an adversarial posture. There’s no question they started it by torturing animals, and I’m grateful that there were people from the beginning standing up and speaking out against it. But what if activism had never put farmers on the defensive, causing them to dig their heels in against even the smallest welfare improvements? Maybe a movement that never conceived of the notion of “animal rights” would have, perversely, achieved more by now, getting more farms to adopt things like cage-free barns and slow-growing chicken breeds.

This isn’t just about some nonexistent past. Opportunities are blossoming now to change how we relate to people who hold the fates of billions of animals in their hands.

Many readers might imagine forming partnerships with the industry in order to develop welfare innovation as a sort of “infiltration,” trying to pull one over on unsuspecting farmers. But it doesn’t have to be like that, and it probably shouldn’t be.

A few weeks ago, I shared this anecdote about a stump speech Paul Shapiro used to give to fiery animal activists. He starts by asking:

How far would you go to achieve animal liberation?

[The crowd cheers.]

Would you do whatever it takes?

Yes! [comes the reply.]

Would you break the law?

[They respond even louder] yes!

Would you go to prison for animals?

Yes!! [It’s fewer voices, but more emphatic.]

Banging his fist on the table: Would you give your life for animals if that’s what it took to win?

Yes! [They scream out in religious fervor!]

[Grabbing the podium like a Baptist preacher, voice thundering out across the crowd]: Alright then. Would you get a hair cut, put on a suit, and go schedule meetings with politicians and corporate boards of directors?

[Quiet murmurs spread across the room as the activists exchange confused looks with one another.]

There’s a version of this dynamic (not with Paul) that I’ve been part of, backstage, after hours, that takes on a darker note, with activists signaling how committed they are to the cause by describing the Machiavellian lengths we would go to if it would help animals. It’s no wonder factory farmers are paranoid about our intentions.

So let me tell you the moment in the last year, maybe in the last ten, where I have felt the most intense respect for an animal advocate, sensed most profoundly the depth of their conviction. It was when a longtime vegan told me they were thinking of starting a factory farm.

It wasn’t a boast, or a naughty secret. It was spoken softly, in the tone of someone about to set out on a secret mission from which they might never return alive. In that instant I knew that if they followed through with it, it would haunt their sleep for the rest of their life. But the vision was worth it: if they could get ahead of the industry, build the new AI-powered farming paradigm that can undercut even the most ruthless factory farms of today, they could shape it to be as good for animals as possible. Success would look like becoming the largest ag company in the world.

Every day, they would hope for cultivated meat to finally arrive, to undercut their product and drive them out of business. But hope doesn’t replicate.

Of course, even if they tried doing this, it probably wouldn’t work out. The baseline probability that your vegan friend is going to become the world’s greatest chicken breast kingpin is low. But what if we didn’t need the chicken farming executives to come from the vegan movement in order to have that kind of relationship with them?

While I was researching this post, I mentioned it to my friend Becca Rogers from New Roots Institute. New Roots doesn’t work on welfare practices directly, so I was surprised when she started rattling off facts I hadn’t heard about how quickly the pork industry in the U.S. is embracing AI. As it turns out, she spends her free time listening to industry podcasts.

I was impressed, even embarrassed; I’ve had the thought before that I should be listening to factory farmers in their own words, as a “know thy enemy” sort of thing. But I could never bring myself to do it. The thought of listening to friendly bumpkins casually chat about torturing animals was too much.

Then I realized that Becca wasn’t thinking of this as infiltration. Yes, farmers’ interests sometimes clash with ours, and when they do we fight for what we want. But if we accept a narrative that sets us invariably at odds, then animals will pay the price for the missed opportunities when our interests could in fact align.

In the height of the Cold War, while they were waging full-on kinetic proxy wars across a dozen countries, the United States and the Soviet Union carried out one of the most complex intergovernmental efforts in history to eradicate smallpox, successfully bringing down the curtain on a disease that claimed 300 million lives in the 20th century, far more than every war combined. The Soviets proposed the program and donated over a billion doses of vaccine; the Americans bankrolled it and led the campaign in the field. The last naturally occurring case was documented and contained inside an active proxy warzone in Somalia. If either country had thumbed its nose at cooperation, they would have wasted countless lives and billions of dollars for no gain.

If that was a one-time miracle, the same dynamic maintains every day between labor unions and large corporate employers. Unions exist primarily to counteract the power of employers, but both sides take their interests too seriously to fail to set their differences aside when those interests align. When foreign competition or new regulations threaten the position of their industry as a whole, labor unions and employer associations fly into D.C. in lockstep. They spend at least as much time cooperating on lobbying and more prosaic tasks like running apprenticeships and co-managing pension funds than they do butting heads in contract negotiations.

When I listened to Becca’s podcast recommendations without assuming hostility, I was surprised how easy it was to imagine myself relating to these farmers in the same way, walking through a farm together inspecting newly-installed welfare equipment, negotiating on the same side of the table as often as on opposite sides. And I could imagine those negotiations leading to bigger wins for animals than anything we’ve achieved thus far.

Can you imagine a world where factory farmers don’t need to be our enemies? Can you imagine how much more influence we could exercise over animals’ lives if we were partners rather than foes?

Can you bring yourself not just to imagine it, but to yearn for it?

Build on,

Sandcastles

–

Easter egg

Regular readers might be interested to know: this article was a step change for me in terms of how I worked with AI. I’ve used Claude to find numbers and citations for me before, but this time Fable spontaneously took a more editorial role, pushing back on lazy rhetoric and suggesting nuanced ways that I could better align my load-bearing arguments with the empirical facts. I imagine this is what it would feel like to work with a professional editor, though I’ve never had that privilege. Only two or three clauses were Claude’s input verbatim, so I expect none of the text to return a positive on Pangram, but writing sentences is the easy part; the contributions Claude did make were more important. If Sandcastles were a newspaper, this is the first piece where I think Claude would have earned a byline. I’m thinking about how to properly acknowledge that in future posts.

This wasn’t long enough for you? Then don’t miss the next one.

Seriously though, I’d really appreciate it if you share this post with someone who might change the course of their advocacy as a result.

Share

item.title: The Campaigner Crunch
item.description: New funding is exacerbating a critical shortage of talent in animal advocacy. How we got here and how we get out.
item.content:encoded:
This is the first of at least two posts on the talent shortage in animal advocacy. This one focuses on the inputs, why we are struggling to find new campaigners. The next post will focus on the nefarious internal conspiracy to steal our best talent away from the top.

In this post:

  • Farmed animal advocacy is in the midst of a significant increase in funding.

  • We are already critically bottlenecked on talent, especially founders and effective campaigners, limiting our ability to make the most of new money.

  • The leadership gap is made wider by several problems:

    • Flagship organizations have stopped investing in the volunteer organizing that produced most of our current campaigners and leaders;

    • We kind of suck at hiring, but it’s haaard; and

    • Our aura is broken, so that many great people don’t want to work on factory farming despite it being OBJECTIVELY THE WORST PROBLEM IN THE WORLD.

  • Who will save us from this talent crisis?

One thing you can do this month to strengthen our leadership pipeline is to attend the Anti-Fur March during Milan Fashion Week on September 26. There is a certain number of attendees at this march that would be enough to win the campaign, toppling one of the last pillars holding up the hated fur industry. The legendary Coalition to Abolish the Fur Trade have computed this number to within a single order of magnitude: somewhere between 1,000 and 10,000. With two weeks to go, there are over 600 people signed up, which you will notice is less than 1,000, but not so much less that your decision to attend wouldn’t make a difference. So join me on an upcoming organizing call with the CAFT team, Sept 14 or 20th at 7:30 pm CET.

But wait, you ask, what does immiserating Milan Fashion Week have to do with our inability to scale insect welfare campaigns? When there are 2gazillion trillion shrimp having their eyes gouged out every second, why even get out of bed for a meager 20 to 100 million foxes, minks and raccoon dogs?

1. Party tricks

Industrial activity requires three elements: land, labor, and capital, the classical economic “factors of production.” Land is necessary to grow or extract natural resources, from wheat and timber to minerals and fuel. Labor converts these raw materials into marketable goods. Capital encompasses the physical and conceptual infrastructure necessary for that conversion, from factory equipment to market position.

Altruistic activity has its own factors of production: people, resources, and strategy. Two thirds match up: to change the world, you need people to do work, and you need money for them to buy things. Besides that, all you need is a good plan.

I recall many late night conversations from years past with fellow animal advocates centered on which of these three factors was our tightest bottleneck to creating more change for animals. About five years ago in particular, it was widely argued that the movement was primarily constrained on funding. With corporate welfare campaigns, this view held, we had finally found a reliable strategy to convert money into change for animals. The formula was so precise, we could hire competent generalists without movement experience to execute on it. In fact, trading in our unwashed punk activists for starched-up professionals with shiny corporate resumés and no visible tattoos would probably be an upgrade. The strategy was solid, the people were out there; we just needed money.

It was not a hard case to make. Factory farming is the worst extant problem in the world even according to conservative assumptions about how much farmed animals can suffer relative to humans. Yet of all charitable dollars, only 1% went to animals, and less than 1% of that 1% went to farmed animals. Animal Charity Evaluators introduced this infamous visualization:

Two things about this graph. First, it’s true, and that is absolutely insane. A catastrophic moral failure by society as a whole. We spent less than $300M fighting factory farming in 2024, barely a third of what Americans spent on Halloween costumes for their pets.

Subscribe now for the hottest trends in companion animal holiday fashion.

Second, though, is that this doesn’t necessarily prove that funding is the main bottleneck for animal advocacy. As pitiably underfunded as we are, we could theoretically be even more impoverished in either of the other factors of altruism: capable, motivated people, and strategies that can scale.

Even five years ago, I often found myself arguing this was the case. It may have just been my contrarian streak, but I think it was due to my experience in the grassroots wing of the animal movement. At its best, the grassroots thrives at mobilizing large numbers of volunteers to sacrifice their free time, among other things, to the cause. I’d seen this work wonders in the golden years of DxE, the Save movement, and Anonymous for the Voiceless, all of which peaked in participation around 2018. I thought that if we played our cards right, we could generate that kind of enthusiasm again, unlocking a lot of capacity for the movement without extra money. I’d even seen larger budgets make some organizations less effective, not just per dollar but in total. As DxE’s budget grew, we became less resourceful, less creative about how to make awesome things happen with volunteers. Money meant there was something to fight over, intensifying power struggles within and between grassroots groups.

This made a great party trick: whenever me and my grassroots friends argued to a room full of funders that the movement was, if anything, overcapitalized, that our true bottleneck was leadership capacity, you could hear jaws hit the floor.

2. Mo’ money, mo’ problems

Those days are gone.

Two things have changed. First is the wave of new funding expected to reach animal welfare next year from the IPOs of major AI companies staffed by effective altruists. We shouldn’t overstate this philanthropic windfall; donors from OpenAI and Anthropic could double the budget of farmed animal advocacy, but we can’t count on anything like pet Halloween costume money, let alone dog and cat rescue charity money. (To all the journalists lurking around for stories about tech billionaires1 imposing basic decency on unwitting American meat consumers, you’re all lying bastard sharks and the deepest ring of hell is waiting for you.)

Nobody knows for sure how much money new donors will bring into animal welfare in the coming years, but even the lowest estimates would be enough to fund basically the entire menu of programs that people had in mind five years ago when talking about animal advocacy being funding constrained.

Once again, that alone doesn’t mean the movement isn’t funding constrained. In the limit, enough money could replace the other factors of altruistic production entirely. With trillions of dollars a year, we could just pay everyone to stop eating meat. With tens of billions, we could buy the genetics companies that breed nearly every animal in industrial farms, and replace the current breeds with genetically engineered painless animals.

The same fanciful dynamic could apply in reverse; a mass social movement on the scale Black Lives Matter could transform public opinion without spending a penny. That’s what I used to mean when I thought about the people factor. Unfortunately, the astute reader might notice that a major shift in public opinion around animal rights would apparently be necessary before millions of people would take to the street. Years of trying to spark a mass movement have moderated my expectations of the scale of public mobilization possible for animals in the short term (and maybe ever) from hundreds of thousands to mere thousands.2 Now when I think about people, I’m more focused on the remarkable achievements a few highly determined campaigners can make when equipped with the right skills, resources, and strategy. (Throughout this post, I use campaign and campaigner in a broad sense, inclusive of most/all frontline work.)

The practical question we face is what to prioritize to make the most of what we will have. What’s the best we can do with a billion dollars? And could we create twice as much impact—or even more—with two billion?

That brings us to the second change since five years ago. The leadership crisis that was simmering then has reached a vigorous boil.

3. Pulling up the ladder

I often talk to job seekers who are understandably confused by two conflicting messages. On one hand, they’ve heard the movement is talent constrained. Yet remote job postings are fiercely competitive, often attracting hundreds of applicants. How to square these two?

There are different types of talent. If I could only add one wrinkle to our three factors of altruistic production—people, resources, and strategy— it would be to subdivide people into leadership and specialists. Specialists have expertise in narrow technical domains, from graphic design and digital marketing to engineering and biotech. There are some technical roles we have a hard time filling, but we are much more constrained by the other type of talent.

By leadership, I don’t necessarily mean the ability to oversee a large organization. I mean people who have the grit to forge a path nobody has gone down before. Founders are usually generalists; they aren’t defined by any hard skill so much as an obsessive, relentless drive to teach themselves whatever skills they will need to succeed at the task they have set out on. And like for-profit entrepreneurs, they usually spend months or years hacking away at their vision before ever seeing their first paycheck.

Campaigning sounds like a specific role on the surface, but it turns out to match the skill profile of the founder. Every campaign is unique, and great campaigners are defined by tenacity and improvisation more than by any hard skill.

Founders and campaigners are the people who turn money into impact for animals. Without them, an extra billion dollars will sit there gathering interest.

Where will we find new leadership capacity? Think of an animal advocate you deeply admire, someone who has made real change for animals during their life. Chances are, that person has made the movement their career, and now takes a modest salary for helping animals– but they started out as a volunteer, organizing a local group or a club on campus, or volunteering/interning with some organization’s campaign. Nearly every important leader I can think of in the movement climbed this ladder; almost none got their start through an open hiring round.

But a few years ago, those leaders made a crucial mistake and pulled the ladder up behind them, making it harder to follow in their footsteps.

The discourse about the funding bottleneck was part of a larger trend, which proponents and opponents alike dubbed professionalization. This became a keyword in movement strategy some time in the last decade– and a source of much misunderstanding. When we think of acting more professional, in part we think of showing up to zoom calls on time and dressing appropriately for meetings with politicians. Taking ourselves seriously in this way is something I hope we can all agree on.

But professionalization was also a trojan horse for a more specific set of ideas, which, to differentiate, we’ll call McKinsification after the infamous management consulting firm, avatar of the corporate culture mocked by Dilbert and Office Space. The gospel of McKinsification in animal advocacy held that:

  1. Volunteers are great at showing up to protests to hold signs, but usually can’t be relied on for more complex tasks;

  2. If a paid staff organizer has an option of delegating a task to a volunteer, training them to do it, and holding them accountable for following through on it, it will take less time for the organizer to just do the task themselves;

  3. Now that we’re on the subject, regarding all these people who started out in the movement as fanatically dedicated volunteers and are now managers of large departments or even entire organizations of more than 100 employees… These folks are great and all but most of them don’t have any training in management or leadership, or even any experience working in a proper professional organization. Wouldn’t it be better to just hire MBAs from McKinsey to run these organizations? Surely there are MBAs who care about animals.

  4. OK, we talked to some McKinsey MBAs and they get paid a lot of money. If we want any of them to start work for us—and keep working for us once they settle down and start a family—we need to, like, quadruple our salaries. There are a few very capable people willing to live like monks in order to campaign for animals, but we’ve already found all of them.

The problem with these commandments was that they were more or less true. Counting on volunteers to execute mission-critical tasks on time is a game of Russian roulette. When it works, it’s the best way for an experienced campaigner to develop new leaders– but even that is costly in the short term, because mentoring people to do things is way more work than just doing them yourself. And when those people are volunteers who may well abandon the project midway and then stop showing up to meetings altogether and never be heard from again, it becomes genuinely hard for managers to sustain.

Worse still, the manager in question is actually just some asshole in their 20s with a music degree and no marketable skills (ahem) who is not obviously qualified to manage anybody.

When Open Philanthropy money first flowed into animal welfare circa 2016, there was really only one way things could go. First, everyone got hired, enabling them to focus their full attention on the cause rather than squeezing it in between food service shifts. Groups that received OP’s blessing like The Humane League, Mercy for Animals, and Anima International flipped from being fueled by 90% volunteer energy to 90% paid staff time. They shifted from an open organizing model—where volunteers could learn the craft of campaigning by owning their own creative projects from start to finish—to a model where volunteers were trusted only to hold signs, join social media comment storms, and occasionally do staff members’ chores.

4. Eating the seed corn

It was at this moment that I got my start in the movement as an organizer with DxE. I encountered a divided movement. Unlike DxE, THL was winning concrete campaigns against large companies. And yet, in a dozen cities across the U.S. where THL had full-time staff members dedicated to volunteer organizing, they could barely turn out five people to a protest with a specific, winnable demand against a corporate target, while DxE chapters consisting entirely of volunteers could get fifty out to a purely symbolic abolitionist protest.

It started to seem like there was an inherent mismatch between discrete, incremental campaigns and volunteer mobilization. Having come into the movement through an organization distinguished by its grandiose rhetoric about completely abolishing all forms of animal exploitation within a single generation, I think I might understand why.

Waking up to the horror of global factory farming is a traumatizing experience. Nobody who pulls the blindfold off, comes to see it for the holocaust it is, wants to hear that we should be calling for anything less than its complete cessation. It can take years of struggle and bitter failure to accept that change might not come so easily. Many people give up at that point, becoming jaded and misanthropic; others become curious about historic efforts, learning how many of our bright ideas have been tried before, learning that many of them failed, but that some achieved incremental progress, progress far short of what you hoped for but far too meaningful to simply ignore.

When there are groups like DxE offering a vision of total societal transformation, the only people who show up for peanuts like cage-free campaigns are those who’ve been around long enough to realize the virtues of incremental persistence– and most of them are already on payroll.

I’m not trying to dodge epistemic accountability here; many people learn those lessons much faster than I did. Organizing in DxE taught me invaluable lessons about making things happen, but it also loaded me up with ideological commitments and self-limiting identities that are taking years to unlearn. If there really is a tension between grassroots activism and disciplined strategic thinking, is volunteer organizing a wise place to recruit campaigners? Or is it just selecting for stubborn ideologues?

I said before that DxE became less resourceful as our budget grew. But money’s indirect effects aren’t all negative; having no money can make it easier to subconsciously treat activism as a game without real consequences.

Anima’s current executive director Jakub Stencel was an early volunteer who participated in the transition from volunteer to professional organization. In his experience, having money in the bank made them feel more concretely the responsibility to deliver change– or at least, it had that effect on some people, which itself became a forcing function for deciding which people to keep around. Helping animals should be enough motivation on its own, but that’s just not how we work, and I agree that having no money in early DxE made it easier to tell ourselves fictions about our theories of change.

So our movement’s current leaders started out as volunteers. What does that prove? Didn’t I just get done saying there was no money to hire anyone before 2016? If so, I misspoke: there have been staff organizations like PETA and HSUS advocating for farmed animals for decades before EA funding created the professional movement landscape we know today. But their most dangerous alumni worked their way up from the lowliest conscripts. In the years that HSUS was rampaging across the country passing historic ballot initiatives culminating in Prop 12, nearly the entire farmed animal department consisted of people who initially met at Compassion Over Killing shortly after it was founded by a high schooler.

By the 20th century, Russian peasants had centuries of experience rationing out a portion of their grain as seeds, keeping enough supply for a few years’ planting in case one harvest was bad. When civil war broke out, military commanders based in the cities couldn’t be bothered with this kind of long-term planning. Both sides of the war sent soldiers into the countryside under their control to violently requisition all seed stores. This provided short-term relief, predictably followed by a devastating famine that killed some five million people, several times more people than died directly in battle.

This not-at-all exaggerated metaphor perfectly describes what happened to our volunteer leadership pipeline in 2016. We hired everyone who could put on a suit, leaving no work to be done by volunteers and no reliable volunteers to do it. The unreliability of volunteers then became a self-fulfilling cycle. We rediscovered one of the most counterintuitive laws of organizing: as two veteran field organizers of Bernie Sanders’ legendary 2016 U.S. presidential campaign put it, more people are willing to do something big than something small. When all that was left for volunteers was holding signs and joining social media comment storms, it’s no wonder we stopped developing new leaders.

Incremental campaign organizations were able to extend their initial wave of professionalization for a couple extra years by plucking campaigners from the ranks of grassroots groups like DxE. But this became less of an option as the two wings drifted apart ideologically; most grassroots abolitionists wanted nothing to do with welfare campaigns, and the feeling was mutual.

Hiring mid-career professionals with no prior experience volunteering or interning in the movement started to look pretty good.

5. McMoral mazes

For several years in the 1980s, sociologist Robert Jackall embedded himself inside the world of corporate middle managers. In the resulting book, Moral Mazes, he described the process by which large hierarchies sever the connection between the quality of your work and your chance of getting promoted. All your boss can see is whether you fit in socially, whether they like you, and most importantly, whether you’ve ever been blamed for something going wrong. Advancement becomes purely a matter of political posturing.

Many participants see the moral maze for what it is and hate every second of it. Some of them eventually decide they don’t want to live their life this way, and come running to the nonprofit sector for redemption. But habits die hard; it’s easier to take the manager out of the maze than vice versa.

When Pro-Animal Future got enough funding to expand beyond our founding team of longtime movement volunteers, I was blown away by the number and quality of applications we got. The most attractive resumes featured advanced degrees and years of professional experience at serious companies; what a surreal experience, I thought, to be interviewing people so much more qualified than myself!

We went through a standard hiring process, culminating in an interview. People interviewed so well that in our first hiring round, we couldn’t narrow down the choices to the two we’d planned to hire, and I opted to go unpaid for an extra year so we could hire three. That turned out not to be necessary; two out of three were gone inside of three months, after clashing sharply with the culture we were trying to build. That two thirds failure rate held across the ten or so of the people we hired through open recruitments over the following years. It took me way too long to realize that the professional credentials I was relying on were almost perfectly inversely correlated with how likely someone was to work out. The people who made it through recruitment without those credentials survived because of a more ineffable culture fit I still haven’t quite managed to put into words, with this essay being my latest failed attempt to do so.

There are people who have made wonderfully successful mid-career pivots into animal advocacy through open hiring rounds, and there are particular experiences I’d be excited to see on a resume now. (For my money, a failed startup/small business founder is worth a hundred MBAs from McKinsey.) But so far, our success with direct hiring has been mostly limited to specialist-type roles. Attempts to fill C-suite leadership roles or general campaigning roles with sparkly corporate resumés as a first point of entry into the movement usually flounder on mission alignment.

That doesn’t mean a McKinsey MBA can never become an animal activist. Mission alignment is not genetically predestined; all of us started outside the movement. It’s about the process we put people through to prepare them for the unique demands of leadership in a moral movement. Mission alignment is a state of mind that can be learned through experiences, just as the mindset of the moral maze can be learned– and unlearned. But it usually takes longer to unlearn habits than to learn them in the first place. The more years of corporate experience on someone’s resume, the more their soul must be purified by the chanting of Hail Marys, by which I mean screaming outside the home of a board member of a company that does business with another company that shares a board member with the company that provides drinking water to the ANIMAL ABUSERS at Milan Fashion Week until your voice grows hoarse.

Rebuilding a serious volunteer leadership pipeline at professional orgs would take a lot of work, not to mention some soul-searching. But the alternatives are at least as onerous, and they aren’t meeting the demand. Anima has responded to the threat of mission drift by building up the most notoriously exhausting recruitment process in animal advocacy. After two rounds of interviews and a suite of test tasks that has taken some applicants an entire week’s worth of full-time work, we subject candidates to a “work trial,” which is more like a marathon final interview where two people—usually including the executive director—spend two full days locked in a room with you plumbing the depths of your soul. It’s an enormous investment of time for everyone involved, and it’s not a formality; most candidates who make it to the work trial get rejected afterwards.

This high fence has kept us culturally aligned– by slowing hiring to a crawl. It is a subject of constant debate inside the organization.

6. Sink or swim

Seeing the inability of campaign organizations to solve the leadership shortage internally, a number of organizations have sprung up to address it at a movement-wide “meta” level. They’ve tried a range of approaches; what has worked?

In his 2014 book Reinventing Organizations, Frederic Laloux recounts the story of a natural experiment in leadership development from a nursing company in The Netherlands. “Neighborhood nurses” have been an important part of the Dutch health care system since the 19th century. For most of that time, they were each independently self-employed, but starting around 1990 they started to be absorbed into the centralized healthcare system. This created efficient economies of scale, but it also removed a personal element of healthcare that many Dutch had come to cherish.

Jos de Blok served as a nurse in this system for more than a decade, seeing firsthand patients’ frustration with the more centralized system before climbing the ladder into managerial functions. Sensing an opportunity for a different kind of nursing company, Jos struck out on his own, founding his own company in 2006. At Jos’s Buurtzorg, nurses would be grouped into small teams that would each cover a handful of neighborhoods, striking a balance between scale and intimacy.

This structure would require a lot of leadership; each team would need someone to take on a founder-like role, taking responsibility for the team’s success. At the start, Jos could oversee all the teams and provide personal mentoring to their leaders. But he had underestimated how dissatisfied nurses were with the existing model; once word got out about Buurtzorg, nurses wanted to join in droves. Before long, there were far more teams than he and the small central admin staff could handle directly.

The experiment happened by accident. Some teams continued receiving hands-on mentorship from the central organization, but past a certain point, new teams were simply given an operating manual and told to sink or swim. They were responsible for doing everything on their own, from recruiting patients to scheduling and billing.

What do you think happened? Were the teams that received hands-on mentorship more successful in the long run, or less?

That’s right: the teams that received more support early on were less successful. They learned from the beginning to be reliant on the central organization to hold their hand through every problem. For the neglected teams, the lack of coddling brought out their latent leadership capacity, forcing themselves to organize around self-sufficiency. De Blok explained to Laloux how he turned this lesson into a primary organizing principle of Buurtzorg:

Coaches shouldn’t have too much time on their hands, or they risk getting too involved with teams, and that would hurt teams’ autonomy. Now they take care of only the most important questions. We gave some of the first teams from Buurtzorg quite intensive support and attention, and today we still see that they are more dependent and less autonomous than other teams.

This anecdote matches my own experience as a social movement organizer. If someone I’m mentoring or managing knows that I’ll step in at the last minute to complete any task they don’t get done, then there’s no shortage of excuses for why they couldn’t get it done this time. I’m sure many of the teams at Buurtzorg that didn’t get coaching eventually failed. But most of those would have failed even with coaching.

That’s the challenging math facing leadership development organizations like Ambitious Impact and New Roots Institute, who have stepped up to try to fill the animal movement’s talent gap. People fall somewhere on this graph:

People above the top line already have what it takes to succeed as founders and campaigners. People below the bottom line just aren’t cut out for it. It’s only in the band between those two lines that a typical structured leadership development program can earn its keep, and that band has proved frustratingly narrow.

The Buurtzorg story points to something that has proven harder for us to provide. People in the top section—our most promising potential recruits—don’t need assigned readings. They need a chance to sink or swim: real targets, real consequences, and a role model they can learn from but who doesn’t have enough spare time to hold their hand.

7. Blessed are the unprofessional

This finally brings us to the miracle of CAFT. The Coalition to Abolish the Fur Trade has achieved what ten years ago seemed impossible: disciplined incremental campaigns powered by large-scale volunteer organizing. They’ve done this by combining an emotionally complete vision—ending the fur trade—with a slowly escalating ladder of corporate targets well matched to their strength. With this coup, CAFT is already breeding the next generation of cracked campaigners.

The synthesis of radical abolitionist rhetoric with focused, winnable campaigns is not itself unprecedented; CAFT is quick to point to the SHAC anti-vivisection campaign of the 90s and oughts as their primary role model, with a few important lessons learned. Yet the movement CAFT is part of has been radically transformed since the SHAC days.

Not only have we professionalized, with larger budgets, more paid staff, and the introduction of a professional managerial culture to varying degrees across organizations; on top of all that, our movement’s standards for impact have increased. This applies equally to the radical wing, which now settles for nothing less than the total eradication of animal farming on short time scales, and to the incremental wing, which has developed a taste for forcing reforms onto the largest multinational food corporations in the world. Neither wing is interested any longer in isolated protests against things like circuses or horse carriages—often the defining animal rights issues of the last century—agreeing that farming should be our main focus.

These transformations have changed what is possible for animal advocacy, for better or worse. I strongly prefer the focus of the current movement, but it faces its own challenges. Among other things, early DxE was defined by a radically accessible organizing model; anybody could seize initiative to try out just about any tactic or strategy as long as they were willing to do the work. It was less an organization and more a platform for independent organizing, and it felt less like volunteering for someone else and more like being an equal part owner of a movement. Most of these autonomous projects failed, but that’s how people learn. It’s how I learned, anyway.

Trying to make sense of why this kind of open organizing rarely survives exposure to even modest amounts of funding has been a focus of Sandcastles. Watching it play out over years as the movement reshaped itself to absorb OP money, I wondered whether that kind of grassroots organizing would ever again be an important part of our story.

CAFT has proved that it can be– and must be. CAFT’s product is not just fur campaigns, but campaigners; a combination of direct work and meta incubation/recruitment. It provides the ideal environment for budding leaders to own projects, to obsess over achieving an outcome, to be shoved out onto the streets with only minimal oversight, to try and fail and try again. Learning to do all of this in service of tangible campaigns that create a feedback loop with reality, they become truly dangerous. That is CAFT’s alchemy.

It’s no accident that all this is happening for fur campaigns. Abolishing fur combines the completeness necessary to motivate optimistic abolitionists with winnable objectives both in the short and medium terms. The fur industry is vulnerable; Poland, the largest fur producer in Europe, last year became the most recent country to pass a ban on new fur farms, with existing farms forced to phase out by 2033. We’re into the stage where every company that drops fur is a meaningful step towards abolition. The strategists behind CAFT aren’t ideological abolitionists, but neither are they tricking anyone into pursuing incrementalism; fur is a topic that different theories of change can honestly agree on.

Like early DxE, all it takes to be part of CAFT is to step up and start organizing protests against designated targets in your city. But that doesn’t mean it’s a free-for-all. The foundational strategy—which fur industry linchpin to target next, and which secondary and tertiary companies to put the screws to—is owned by the central team. But the work of building chapters, recruiting activists, and creatively escalating pressure on those targets falls to largely autonomous local organizers. The structure works, with 60 independent local groups organizing protests haranguing targets across 19 countries in the past six months– all with only 3.5 staff members, collectively paid about as much as two typical junior grantmakers. Before they had the budget to salary even a single member of their core team, CAFT’s late-night protests outside board members’ homes had already won campaigns that evaded large, risk-averse professional organizations for years, extracting fur-free commitments from top luxury brands like Vogue (Condé Nast), Neiman Marcus, and Marc Jacobs.

But the real journey is the friendscampaigners we made along the way. Campaigners like my friend Pips, a former software engineer who volunteered on the periphery of the movement for years until he started joining CAFT’s touring machine, couch-surfing across the U.S. organizing protests. Pips is so much a product of CAFT’s security-minded culture that despite now selling out to run cage-free and shrimp welfare campaigns for ICAW, he still doesn’t use his legal name anywhere (literally, he has stayed at my house for weeks and even I don’t know it). Every one of those local groups counts for at least one person learning the craft of campaigning from the ground up, and Pips is just one of nearly a dozen CAFT alumni to go professional in the last year.

This month, CAFT is building up to their largest mobilization ever, aiming to turn out at least a thousand people to a march on September 26, the height of Milan Fashion Week. (To hear why Milan Fashion Week is such a key pillar of support for the European fur industry that CAFT have been making their lives hell for half a year, join me for one of their upcoming organizing calls.) But they’re doing it the hard way. It really does take more effort to train a new volunteer than to just do things yourself, yet the Milan march and the week of action surrounding it is being pulled together by a local team all volunteering ten to fifty hours a week.

Speaking of which, if you’re looking to hire in Italy, I’d like to introduce you to the newest crop of unstoppable campaigners.

If you’re looking to take the first step onto that well-trodden ladder towards becoming a great activist, CAFT is one of the easiest places to do it: you can join from anywhere in the world and cut your teeth on a systematic campaign while getting support from some of the most obsessed campaigners in the movement.

If you’ve already found your niche in the movement, CAFT deserves your support even more. They are building up the leadership pipeline that all your future plans will rely on. They’re like an open source software project that all the hyperscalers quietly take advantage of; you should give back even for purely selfish reasons!

8. The price of admission

I spent nearly seven years volunteering full time for the movement before I went on a salary. The first three of those, I was living on a college scholarship, neglecting my coursework and borrowing my dad’s Suburban to drive truckloads of college students out on nighttime field trips to factory farms. For the last two, I was living off extended pandemic unemployment, food stamps, and medicaid while my Pax Fauna cofounders were living in spare rooms of my family house and getting paid $30k a year. I spent one year living in a closet and another in a hallway.

I thought these would be the best seven years of my life; every moment of it was a gift.

One takeaway from this would be: you can do it! Make this leap and there is a beautiful life awaiting you. By the time I was finishing college, I had burned up most of my other opportunities through a combination of neglect and a growing criminal record for civil disobedience. I didn’t know how I was going to support myself, but I quickly found there was always a couch to sleep on if I could make myself useful. What I traded in comfort, I more than made back in inspiring friendships, unforgettable adventures, and most of all, a life full of purpose.

But this is not the whole picture. I kept moving for those seven years knowing that if I had ever encountered a crisis, I could have fallen back in a heartbeat on my family, who sit around the 96th percentile of American wealth. I have a low need for comfort; I make $135k in my current role and still choose to share a room in San Francisco with 15 other people. I don’t have pets and I don’t plan to have kids.

If we applied these standards to every would-be campaigner, we would stay small indeed. And we can’t wait seven years or even two years for new talent; we need to grow much faster.

How can we attract more of the people from the top section of the graph from earlier, the people who will start great things without anyone holding their hand? One of the simplest things to try would be increasing salaries. I’ve certainly heard many people cite low pay as the main reason animal advocacy remains a peripheral interest for them. Back when we were primarily bottlenecked on funding, there wasn’t much we could do about that. What about now?

Jakub has told me that for a copy of Anima’s top campaigning guru Thorbjørn Schiønning, he would pay several million dollars a year– more than half the organization’s budget. If great campaigners are worth that much, letting an experienced campaigner leave the movement for a corporate job because their salary is a few tens of thousands of dollars short of what they’d need to start a family is a stupid waste. It would be just as wasteful if someone who would have become a great campaigner spotted that dilemma in advance and opted out before they ever had the chance.

But salaries alone won’t solve our hiring woes. Pay in the movement has gone up dramatically since 2015, and besides the problems already described, it has mostly led to:

  1. internal competition, a price war between animal advocacy orgs fighting over the same limited pool of mission-aligned talent; and

  2. a flood of low-quality applicants to every remote job posting, making it harder to pick out the mission-aligned people without increasing their number by much.

Low pay, and especially common knowledge of low pay, contributes to a deeper problem: for the kind of highly ambitious, entrepreneurial people we need as founders and campaigners, animal advocacy is seen as low status. Most people don’t think of it so explicitly– which is why it has an effect on them. The kind of people who might dedicate their career to animals don’t want to think of themselves as status seekers, but at some point, you have to imagine telling your parents that you’re giving up on your ambitious career path of becoming a doctor/lawyer/engineer to fight for the political rights of their lunch meat.

This will be true to some extent as long as society fundamentally does not value the lives of animals, which I expect will be ~forever. But there are things we can do to counteract it.

I wish more people knew that it’s possible to earn well over $200,000 by becoming one of the absolute best animal welfare campaigners. I bet you didn’t even know that. But it’s true!3 Not all of the top campaigners make that much, but some of them do. I want more of them to, and I want that to become widely known. I want people to grind a bit harder knowing that they could earn that much if they hone their skills to such a high level.

For some people, status comes not just from salary, but from working on the world’s most important and neglected problem. Factory farming remains undefeated in this regard, though a pesky challenger has emerged in the form of AI safety. The field of AI safety has stolen all the aura in effective altruism. This is painfully ironic; it means that the AI researchers donating millions of dollars to animal welfare simultaneously created the problem that is stealing away so many young altruists, making it impossible for us to spend those millions on new campaigners and founders.

Working in AI safety promises a special kind of intellectual glamor. Your name will be published on splashy research papers, regardless of whether that research has any hope of steering the development of AI. You’ll work at a desk with a magnificent view of the San Francisco Bay, in a luxurious office packed with complementary food and ivy league grads who’ve read the same sci-fi books as you.

There’s something wrong will all of this. Deeply wrong. But I’m not going to explain it until the next post. So for now, you’ll just have to take my word for it:

Only soyboy beta cucks would work on AI safety instead of animal welfare.

The end

I’m painfully aware that everything I’ve laid out here doesn’t add up to a solution that will bring in enough new leaders. That means it’s all the more incumbent on you to forge your own path in. Don’t wait for permission; nobody has time to give it to you.

Unless you meet me in Milan, I can definitely give it to you there.
